d: Christopher Columbus makes landfall in the Caribbean, initiating transatlantic contact between Europe and the Americas.
Spain and Portugal agreed by treaty to divide newly discovered lands along a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, moving westward the line Pope Alexander VI had drawn in 1493.
A royal order authorized the governor of Hispaniola to grant Spanish colonists the labor of indigenous people in exchange for their Christianization.

Spanish conquistador Francisco Vásquez de Coronado led an expedition through the American Southwest from 1540 to 1542, documenting Pueblo communities and other indigenous societies with sophisticated agricultural systems, trade networks, and political organizations.
A theological debate between Bartolomé de Las Casas and Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda addressed the rights and humanity of indigenous peoples.
Sir Walter Raleigh attempted to establish the first permanent English settlement in the Americas.
Juan de Oñate brutally crushed Pueblo resistance at Acoma in modern-day New Mexico.
The Virginia Company established the first permanent English settlement in North America.

t: French Settlement at Quebec / Samuel Champlain Founds Quebec
d: Samuel Champlain established Quebec as a fur-trading post, anchoring French colonization efforts on commerce and indigenous alliances rather than territorial conquest and large-scale European settlement.

t: First Enslaved Africans Arrive in Virginia
d: The privateer White Lion landed roughly twenty African captives at Point Comfort in late August, trading them to Virginia officials in exchange for badly needed provisions.
Virginia's first elected assembly, later called the House of Burgesses, met in the Jamestown church with two burgesses chosen from each of the colony's settlements.
Pilgrims aboard the Mayflower signed a self-governing agreement establishing a democratic colony in Plymouth.

Director Peter Minuit of the Dutch West India Company established New Amsterdam on Manhattan Island as the principal settlement of the New Netherland colony, transforming it into a vital trading hub for North American furs and goods destined for European markets.
Puritans led by John Winthrop launched a large-scale religious settlement in New England.

t: Roger Williams Banned / Rhode Island Founded
d: Dissident minister Roger Williams, sentenced to banishment from Massachusetts in October 1635 for advocating separation of church and state, fled south and founded Providence in 1636.
Colonial law guaranteed religious freedom to all Trinitarian Christians in Maryland.
England enacted mercantilist laws requiring colonial trade to flow through English ships and ports.

t: Virginia Establishes Hereditary Slavery Through Maternal Descent
d: Virginia's House of Burgesses passes an act declaring that children born to enslaved mothers inherit enslaved status for life, institutionalizing hereditary, permanent slavery as a generational condition tied to maternal descent.

t: English Capture of New Amsterdam (New York)
d: English naval forces seized the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam without firing a shot.

English settlers, many of them planters relocating from Barbados, founded Charles Town in Carolina. They carried the West Indian plantation model with them, and the colony grew into the staple-crop, slave-labor society that defined the southern colonial region.
A multi-tribal alliance attacked New England towns in the bloodiest per-capita colonial conflict.
Nathaniel Bacon led armed Virginia colonists against Governor Berkeley and Native Americans on the frontier.
Popé and allied Pueblo communities launched a coordinated uprising across New Mexico in August 1680, killing roughly 400 colonists and driving Spanish survivors south to El Paso.
William Penn established a proprietary colony as a refuge for Quakers based on religious tolerance.

t: Glorious Revolution / English Bill of Rights
d: England's Protestant monarchs William and Mary accepted parliamentary supremacy, reshaping colonial charters.
A wave of witchcraft accusations in Salem, Massachusetts led to twenty executions.
About twenty enslaved people, led by a man called Jemmy, seized weapons near the Stono River in South Carolina and marched south toward Spanish Florida, gathering some sixty followers.
A wave of emotional Protestant revivals swept the colonies through the 1730s and 1740s, cresting around 1740 as George Whitefield drew enormous crowds on his preaching tours.
Seven colonies met to coordinate defense against France and secure Iroquois loyalty ahead of the French and Indian War.
Britain and its colonial allies defeated France and its Native allies in a conflict over North American territory.
A Native American alliance attacked British forts while King George III banned colonial settlement west of the Appalachians.
Britain imposed a direct tax on printed materials in the colonies to help pay war debts.
British soldiers fired into a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people.
Colonial protesters dumped 342 chests of British East India Company tea into Boston Harbor.
Twelve colonies met in Philadelphia to organize a unified response to British punishments.
The first military engagements of the Revolutionary War between British troops and colonial militias.

t: Abigail Adams Advocates for Women's Rights
d: In a letter to her husband during the Continental Congress, Abigail Adams urged protection of women's rights and legal status in the new republic, famously asking him to 'remember the ladies' in the laws of the new nation.
The Second Continental Congress formally declared the thirteen colonies independent from Britain.
Continental forces surrounded and captured a major British army in upstate New York.

Pennsylvania's legislature passed the first gradual abolition law in the United States, providing for the eventual emancipation of enslaved people. The law reflected revolutionary ideals of natural rights and human equality.
The first U.S. constitution created a weak central government with most power reserved to the states.
The peace treaty ending the Revolutionary War granted formal British recognition of U.S. independence.
An armed uprising of indebted western Massachusetts farmers exposed the fatal weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation.
Delegates meeting in Philadelphia discarded the Articles of Confederation and wrote a new federal constitution.
The Confederation Congress created an orderly process for admitting new states from the territory north of the Ohio River, and banned slavery there.
Nine states ratified the new Constitution, replacing the Articles of Confederation.
Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton proposed paying federal debt at full value and having the national government assume the states' Revolutionary War debts to establish public credit.
The first ten amendments to the Constitution guaranteed individual liberties and limited federal power.
Eli Whitney built a machine that stripped seeds from short-staple cotton, cleaning roughly fifty times what a worker could process by hand in a day.
Western Pennsylvania farmers violently protested an excise tax on whiskey.

t: Alien and Sedition Acts & Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions
d: Federalists passed four laws targeting immigrants and press criticism of the government; Jefferson and Madison replied with resolutions claiming states could judge federal laws unconstitutional.
Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson defeated Federalist John Adams in the first peaceful transfer of power between opposing parties.
The United States purchased approximately 828,000 square miles from France, doubling the nation's size.
Supreme Court Chief Justice John Marshall struck down a section of the Judiciary Act of 1789, establishing judicial review.
Jefferson banned all American exports to foreign ports in response to British and French violations of free seas.
The United States declared war on Britain over impressment of sailors and British support for Native American resistance.
Andrew Jackson's forces won a crushing military victory over veteran British forces after the peace treaty had already been signed.
The Supreme Court unanimously upheld Congress's power to charter the Second Bank of the United States and voided Maryland's tax on its Baltimore branch.
Congress admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, drawing a line at 36°30'.

The Merrimack Manufacturing Company began operating textile mills at Lowell, Massachusetts, scaling the integrated factory system pioneered at Waltham into the largest manufacturing complex in the country. The "Lowell system" recruited unmarried young women from New England farms as wage laborers, housing them in company boardinghouses.
President Monroe declared the Western Hemisphere closed to further European colonization or intervention.
John Quincy Adams won the presidency in the House of Representatives over Andrew Jackson in a controversial deal.
A state-funded canal connected the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean via the Hudson River, cutting shipping costs by 90%.

Andrew Jackson defeated incumbent John Quincy Adams in a decisive victory that reflected the growing electoral power of common white men without property. Jackson's triumph demonstrated the practical effects of expanded suffrage and marked the emergence of modern mass politics.
Congress authorized the forced relocation of Native American tribes from the Southeast to lands west of the Mississippi.
Decades of Protestant revivalism, building from the early 1800s and cresting around 1830, spread camp meetings and the conviction that salvation was an individual choice.
William Lloyd Garrison began publishing an abolitionist weekly in Boston on January 1, 1831, demanding immediate and unconditional emancipation rather than gradual reform.
Enslaved preacher Nat Turner led a bloody organized slave uprising in Virginia, killing 60 white people.
South Carolina declared federal tariffs null, void, and non-binding within its state borders.

t: Calhoun's "Slavery as a Positive Good" Speech
d: Senator John C. Calhoun of South Carolina delivered an influential congressional address arguing that slavery was a positive moral and social institution, marking a decisive shift from earlier gradualist defenses toward celebration of slavery.
Federal troops herded Cherokee families into stockades beginning in May 1838, then forced roughly 16,000 people west to Indian Territory over the following winter.
The U.S. admitted the Lone Star Republic as a state via a joint resolution of Congress.
Armed conflict between the U.S. and Mexico fought across Texas, California, and Central Mexico.
A proposed legislative amendment sought to ban slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico.
Mass migration of 300,000 'Forty-Niners' rushed to California following gold discovery at Sutter's Mill.
The first women's rights convention produced the Declaration of Sentiments demanding equality for women.
A series of acts admitted California as a free state and strengthened the Fugitive Slave Law.
Harriet Beecher Stowe's anti-slavery novel sold millions of copies and transformed northern public opinion on slavery.
Congress repealed the Missouri Compromise and allowed popular sovereignty to determine slavery in new territories.
The Supreme Court ruled that African Americans were not citizens and Congress could not ban slavery in territories.

t: John Brown's Raid on Harpers Ferry
d: Radical abolitionist John Brown attempted to seize a federal arsenal to initiate an armed slave revolt.
Republican candidate Lincoln won the presidency without winning a single southern state.

t: Secession and the Firing on Fort Sumter
d: Six seceded states formed the Confederacy at Montgomery in February, joined by Texas in March, and in April Confederate batteries bombarded the federal garrison holding Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor.
Congress offered 160-acre plots to settlers who farmed them for five years and authorized the Union Pacific and Central Pacific to build a transcontinental railroad.
President Lincoln declared enslaved people in Confederate states to be free as a war measure.

t: Battle of Gettysburg & the Gettysburg Address
d: Union forces repulsed Lee's invasion of Pennsylvania in a three-day July battle, and that November Lincoln spoke at the dedication of the soldiers' cemetery there.

t: Black Codes and the Rise of Sharecropping
d: Southern states enacted Black Codes to restrict freedpeople's rights and labor mobility. Unable to acquire land through the failed federal redistribution, formerly enslaved people entered into sharecropping contracts that bound them to plantation labor and debt cycles, perpetuating economic subjugation.
Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands inside the War Department to aid formerly enslaved people and destitute refugees across the ruined South.
General Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to General Ulysses S. Grant, effectively ending the Civil War.
The amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime.
The amendment granted citizenship to formerly enslaved people and guaranteed equal protection under the law.
The Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads met at Promontory Summit, Utah, connecting the continent by rail.
Ratified on February 3, 1870, the amendment barred the federal government and the states from denying the vote based on race, color, or previous enslavement.
Lakota Sioux and Cheyenne warriors destroyed General Custer's 7th Cavalry in Montana.
An informal political deal awarded the contested 1876 presidency to Republican Rutherford B. Hayes in exchange for ending Reconstruction.
A nationwide strike halted rail traffic and was crushed by federal troops sent by President Hayes.

t: Thomas Edison Perfects the Incandescent Light Bulb
d: Thomas Edison developed a durable, commercially viable incandescent electric lamp, leading to the rapid electrification of American cities, homes, and factories.

t: Frances Willard Leads Women's Christian Temperance Union
d: Frances Willard became president of the Women's Christian Temperance Union and transformed it into the largest women's organization in America, connecting temperance to campaigns for women's suffrage and political equality.
A federal law halted all immigration of Chinese laborers into the United States.

t: Standard Oil Trust & the Rise of Big Business
d: John D. Rockefeller's lawyers placed dozens of allied oil companies under nine trustees, inventing a legal device that centralized control of an industry across state lines.
A bomb was thrown at police during a labor rally in Chicago; police opened fire, killing workers.
A law broke up communal tribal lands into individual private 160-acre farming plots to force assimilation.

t: Jane Addams Founds Hull House Settlement
d: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr established Hull House in a poor Chicago neighborhood, creating a model settlement house that provided social services, education, and advocacy for immigrant communities.
Congress passed the first federal law to limit monopolies and protect competitive markets.
U.S. Army soldiers opened fire on a camp of Lakota Sioux, killing nearly 300 men, women, and children.
The federal immigration station in New York Harbor opened on January 1, 1892, receiving arrivals who came increasingly from southern and eastern Europe.
Steelworkers battled armed Pinkerton detectives at Andrew Carnegie's steel mill in Pennsylvania.
A third-party political convention demanded radical economic reforms for farmers and workers.

The World's Columbian Exposition opened in Chicago on May 1, 1893, presenting innovative technologies, consumer goods, and leisure activities to millions of middle-class visitors. The fair showcased modern retail concepts and luxury goods, reinforcing consumer culture as central to middle-class identity and promoting new forms of urban entertainment and commercial display.
Railroad workers boycotted Pullman luxury cars, halting western rail traffic before being ended by a federal court injunction.

t: Atlanta Compromise: Washington vs. Du Bois
d: Booker T. Washington told a mostly white Atlanta exposition audience that Black Southerners should build trades and property before pressing claims to social and political equality.
William Jennings Bryan's free-silver oratory captured the Democratic nomination, but Republican William McKinley's lavishly funded campaign carried the industrial North and the presidency.
The Supreme Court ruled that racially segregated public facilities did not violate the 14th Amendment.
The U.S. defeated Spain in a brief war, gaining Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines.
The U.S. issued diplomatic notes demanding equal trading access to China for all the major powers, including Japan alongside Britain, Germany, Russia, France, and Italy.
Roosevelt pressed coal operators and striking miners into arbitration and sued the Northern Securities railroad combination, casting the presidency as a neutral referee between capital and labor.

t: Meat Inspection Act & Pure Food and Drug Act
d: Federal laws regulated consumer health standards and food production facilities.
An industrial disaster in New York City killed 146 young immigrant garment workers.
A central national bank was created while the income tax and direct election of senators were ratified.
Black southerners left the rural South for northern and midwestern cities in rising numbers after 1916, part of a movement that continued for decades.

t: Espionage and Sedition Acts & Schenck v. United States
d: The 1917 Espionage Act and its 1918 Sedition Act amendments criminalized anti-war speech, and in 1919 the Supreme Court ruled in Schenck v. United States that speech posing a 'clear and present danger' could be restricted.
President Woodrow Wilson asked Congress for a declaration of war against Germany.
Attorney General Palmer deported hundreds of suspected radicals without trial.

t: Treaty of Versailles & Rejection of the League of Nations
d: The treaty ending World War I was signed in June 1919, but the Senate refused to ratify it and kept the United States out of the League of Nations.
Women gained the constitutional right to vote in all U.S. elections.
KDKA Pittsburgh launched the first regularly scheduled commercial radio broadcasts in 1920, initiating the era of radio as a mass medium for entertainment and news.

t: Washington Naval Conference & Naval Arms Limitation
d: The Washington Naval Conference (1921-1922) produced treaties limiting naval construction and establishing Pacific power arrangements, exemplifying the U.S. interwar approach to international order without the League of Nations.
Immigration law established a strict 2% quota based on the 1890 census to restrict immigration.
Tennessee teacher John Scopes was tried in July 1925 for teaching evolution, in a nationally publicized courtroom clash over science, religion, and modern life.
A sudden, catastrophic collapse of prices on the New York Stock Exchange triggered the Great Depression.
FDR launched sweeping federal programs to provide relief, recovery, and reform during the Great Depression.

t: Social Security Act & the Second New Deal
d: Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act in August 1935, pairing old-age pensions and unemployment insurance with the WPA's jobs program in a bolder phase of the New Deal.
Japan's surprise attack on the U.S. naval base brought America into World War II.
120,000 Japanese-Americans were forcibly relocated to inland concentration camps.

t: D-Day and the Liberation of Western Europe
d: Allied forces landed on five Normandy beaches on June 6, 1944, opening the long-delayed western front against Nazi Germany.

t: Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
d: The U.S. dropped two atomic weapons on Japanese cities, forcing unconditional surrender.

In February 1945, President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, and Soviet Leader Joseph Stalin convened at Yalta in Crimea to negotiate the postwar world order. The leaders discussed the founding of the United Nations, the occupation and reparations for Germany, Soviet entry into the Pacific War against Japan in exchange for territorial concessions in Asia, and the political future of Eastern Europe and Poland. The conference represented the apex of the Grand Alliance and the dominant U.S. role in shaping postwar peace settlements.
The U.S. pledged military aid to anti-communist nations and gave $13 billion to rebuild war-torn Western Europe.
The United States and eleven allies signed the North Atlantic Treaty in April 1949, while Allied planes supplied West Berlin through a Soviet blockade lifted that May, flying on until September.
A Cold War proxy conflict ended in a stalemate at the 38th parallel.
Senator Joseph McCarthy claimed in February 1950 to hold a list of communists working inside the State Department, fueling years of loyalty investigations and blacklisting.
The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional.
A year-long economic protest by Black citizens resulted in the desegregation of city buses.

President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, authorizing construction of a 41,000-mile Interstate Highway System. This legislation represented the largest federal infrastructure investment in American history and directly enabled mass suburban expansion, automobile-centered consumer culture, and broad-based economic growth through construction employment and related industries.

t: Rock and Roll Challenge to Cultural Conformity
d: Rock and roll music, popularized by performers like Elvis Presley, Chuck Berry, and Little Richard, challenged postwar cultural conformity and emerged as a symbol of youth rebellion. Elvis's controversial television performances sparked moral panics among adults over music's influence on sexual behavior and race relations.
Nine Black teenagers enrolled at all-white Central High School in Arkansas, and army paratroopers escorted them to class past a hostile white mob.
The Soviet Union placed the first artificial satellite in orbit, and its steady radio beeps convinced Americans that Moscow had seized the technological lead.
CIA-backed Cuban exiles attempted to overthrow Fidel Castro, but Kennedy withdrew air support and the invasion collapsed. The fiasco strengthened Castro and drove Cuba closer to Soviet alliance.
A tense 13-day nuclear standoff between the U.S. and the Soviet Union over missiles in Cuba.
About 250,000 demonstrators gathered at the Lincoln Memorial on August 28, 1963, demanding civil rights legislation and economic opportunity for Black Americans.
Landmark legislation outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.
Congress authorized the President to take all necessary measures in Vietnam after alleged attacks on U.S. destroyers.
Johnson drove a sweeping reform program through Congress in 1965, creating Medicare and Medicaid and sending the first large federal aid to public schools.
Signed at the foot of the Statue of Liberty in October 1965, Hart-Celler scrapped the national origins quotas and replaced them with hemispheric caps and family preferences.
Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on August 6, 1965, suspending literacy tests and sending federal examiners into Southern counties that had long blocked Black registration.
A massive coordinated surprise assault by North Vietnamese and Vietcong forces across South Vietnam shattered public support for the war.

t: Earth Day & the Creation of the EPA
d: Some 20 million Americans joined the first Earth Day in April 1970, and the Environmental Protection Agency began operating that December.
Nixon spent a week in China in February 1972, ending more than two decades of American nonrecognition and opening a period of eased Cold War tensions.
Arab oil producers cut shipments to the United States in October 1973 over its support for Israel, driving fuel prices up and deepening a decade of stagflation.
A treaty ended direct United States military involvement in the Vietnam War.
The Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional right to privacy protected a woman's right to choose an abortion.
Richard Nixon became the first U.S. president to resign from office amid the Watergate scandal.
Iranian radicals seized the U.S. embassy in Tehran, holding 52 Americans hostage for 444 days.
Conservative Republican Ronald Reagan defeated incumbent Democrat Jimmy Carter in a landslide.
The peaceful destruction of the physical barrier separating East and West Berlin symbolized the collapse of Soviet communism.
A U.S.-led coalition drove Iraqi forces out of Kuwait in a six-week air campaign followed by a brief ground war.
The Soviet Union dissolved into fifteen independent republics, ending the Cold War.

California voters approved Proposition 187, a ballot initiative that would restrict public services and benefits to undocumented immigrants and their children, igniting national debate over immigration policy and demographic change.
NAFTA took effect on January 1, 1994, phasing out tariffs among the United States, Canada, and Mexico and creating one of the world's largest trading blocs.
Al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four commercial airplanes, destroying the World Trade Center towers and damaging the Pentagon.

t: Election of Barack Obama & The Great Recession
d: The first African-American president was elected amidst the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.
